lessonRef.title: Writing plan and draft: planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it

studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it within the unit “Summary and Theme: Saying What a Story Means.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's writing plan and draft work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] At the community garden, Priya opened a folder containing a draft whose final paragraph changes its purpose. A note on the cover read “Summary and Theme: Saying What a Story Means,” but the pages inside told one unfinished story. Priya expected the ending to explain everything. Instead, the first scene offered only a quiet choice: return a borrowed object without comment or admit why it had been kept.

[2] The main character rehearsed an apology three times. In the first version, every sentence began with “I.” In the second, the character blamed the confusing rules. In the third, the character named the harm, returned the object, and then stopped talking. The narrator never announced which version was sincere.

[3] Xavier noticed that a repeated image—a door left slightly open—appeared before each rehearsal. At first it seemed like background description. By its third appearance, the image could suggest an invitation, an escape, or an unfinished decision. The story gave enough detail to support more than one interpretation but not enough to make every interpretation equally strong.

[4] The final scene ended before the apology was delivered. Priya argued that the missing speech made the character seem afraid; Xavier thought the pause showed care. To connect the scene to planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it, each reader had to identify exact language, explain an inference, and account for the detail that made the other reading possible.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 30: planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 30: planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it,” then answer: Draft the planned response about planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it. How will each paragraph use the reading rather than merely mention it?

Deliverable: Grade 4: a complete first draft with source-based development in every body section; write two connected paragraphs.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 30: planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 30: planning a summary-and-theme response for a reader who has not read it.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
